Container.Name: textymcspeechy
Container.Overview:
Train your own Piper TTS voice on your Unraid server's NVIDIA GPU. Give it a folder of speech recordings and a transcript, and it produces a Piper .onnx voice you can drop straight into Home Assistant.
Self-contained: pull, apply, go. No local image build, no host packages, no scripts to install. Everything runs inside the container.
HOW TO USE IT: click the WebUI button. Drop in one long recording — an interview, a podcast episode, a couple of hours is fine — and press a button. It is split into clips and transcribed automatically, and clips are grouped by who is speaking, so on a two-person podcast you keep only your target speaker in one click.
You then review the clips in the browser: play each one, fix any transcription mistakes, and exclude the ones you do not want. Getting the transcripts right is the single biggest factor in how good the finished voice sounds, so this step is built to be fast — J and K move, Space plays, E includes or excludes, Enter edits.
When you are happy, press Start training. The web UI shows live progress, and once checkpoints appear you can type a sentence and hear what the voice sounds like at each one. That is how you decide it is done. Training keeps running if you close the tab.
Prefer a terminal? Everything is also available through the `tms` command on the container console — run `tms` for the list, or `tms doctor` to check the GPU.
REQUIREMENTS: an NVIDIA GPU and the Unraid Nvidia-Driver plugin, with "--runtime=nvidia" left in Extra Parameters. RTX 50-series (Blackwell) cards need a recent driver branch built from NVIDIA's open kernel modules — if `nvidia-smi` on the Unraid terminal does not list your card, fix that first. `tms doctor` checks all of this in a few seconds.
STORAGE: the image is large (~15GB) and training needs room to work — budget 50GB free. Point the appdata path at an NVMe pool rather than the array, and set that share to Cache: Only so the mover cannot relocate an active training run.
MEMORY CAP: Extra Parameters limits the container to 24g with swap disabled (--memory-swap set equal to --memory). The cap stops a runaway run starving the rest of the server; disabling swap matters just as much, because a training run that spills to swap does not fail, it crawls -- the GPU sits idle waiting on disk for hours. Failing fast is the better outcome.
Two things to know about that limit: the 8g of shared memory counts toward it, and raising PIPER_BATCH_SIZE raises host RAM use as well as VRAM. If a run dies with "DataLoader worker (pid N) is killed by signal", that is this cap rather than a bug. Run `docker stats textymcspeechy` during training to see actual use, then set the cap to roughly 1.5x the peak.
FIRST RUN: pretrained checkpoints are a separate ~5GB download that training builds on. Get them with `tms checkpoints en-us` on the console. The web UI warns you if they are missing. Speech recognition models also download on first import (~3GB) into appdata, not into the image.
Ports below: 8080 is the web UI. 6006 is TensorBoard for loss curves, which only answers while training is running.
Container.Requires: An NVIDIA GPU and the Unraid Nvidia-Driver plugin.

Config.Name: Appdata
Config.Description: Everything you make lives here: datasets, pretrained checkpoints, training workspaces and finished voices. It is populated automatically on first start. Put it on an NVMe pool set to Cache: Only — training reads the dataset constantly and writes ~800MB checkpoints every couple of epochs, and the mover relocating that mid-run will bring training to a crawl. Budget 50GB.

Config.Name: Nvidia GPU UUID
Config.Description: Which GPU to use. 'all' is right if you have one NVIDIA card. With more than one, paste the GPU-xxxxxxxx-... UUID from Settings -> Nvidia Driver so this container cannot take the card your transcoder or VM is using.

Config.Name: Nvidia driver capabilities
Config.Description: What the container may use the driver for. compute,utility is CUDA plus nvidia-smi, which is everything training needs. Do not add 'video' — that is for transcoding.

Config.Name: PUID
Config.Description: User ID that owns the voices and datasets this container creates. 99 is Unraid's 'nobody' — keeping it means your files look like everything else on the array and stay readable over SMB.

Config.Name: PGID
Config.Description: Group ID for created files. 100 is Unraid's 'users'.

Config.Name: UMASK
Config.Description: File creation mask. 000 makes finished voices group- and other-writable, which is usually what you want for files you will copy off over SMB. Use 022 to tighten it.

Config.Name: TZ
Config.Description: Timezone, e.g. Europe/London. Only affects log and checkpoint timestamps.

Config.Name: Run as root
Config.Description: Leave false. Set true only if you are compiling custom espeak-ng pronunciation rules, which genuinely need root inside the container. Everything created while this is on will be root-owned.

Config.Name: WebUI
Config.Description: The web interface: import a recording, review and correct the transcriptions, then train and listen to the result. This is the main way to use the container.

Config.Name: TensorBoard
Config.Description: TensorBoard, for watching loss curves while training. Nothing listens here when idle, so a refused connection between runs is expected.
